Interpretable defect detection for hot-rolled steel

YOLO26n detection · Proto-BagNet classification · MSc dissertation, 2026

Problem

Post-hoc methods, such as EigenCAM, have been applied to YOLO-based detection in defect detection, with conclusions that the model effectively identified defect regions on visual heatmap inspection, without empirically evaluating whether those regions genuinely drove detection. With randomisation of network weights, post-hoc attribution maps remained visually unchanged, concluding that post-hoc visual heatmaps can be misleading.

Approach

To tackle this, I experimented with a prototype-based learner, Proto-BagNet, bolted onto YOLO26’s classification decision after the bounding box has been produced.

Hypothesis

If you embed an interpretable-by-design prototype patch learner into training, the model will classify decisions and show the patch from the training data it used to classify.

Results

Each detection comes back with its crop, the prototype patch it matched, and the similarity map that produced the score. When removing highlighted regions, the classification changed, demonstrating interpretability during the model forward pass.

Edge-deployed leak detection for urban water networks

NSGA-II · autoencoder · GCN · L-Town benchmark · University of Bath, 2026

Problem

Acoustic leak detection is slow and gives no real-time monitoring of underground leaks.

Approach

A three-stage pipeline per DMA zone: NSGA-II sensor placement, edge autoencoder detection, cloud GCN localisation.

Leak localisation

On an alert, the GCN takes pressure and demand at each junction, passes them along the pipe network through two graph layers, and scores every junction; the highest score is the leak. Gradients of that score give a pipe-segment risk map.

Results

22 sensors instead of 33 at 90.7% coverage. Leaks detected at 92.0% TPR and 1.4% FPR. Leak junction found in 72% of tests (93% top five), mean error 65.8 m.

Closed-loop melt pool depth control for LPBF

Group project · MeltpoolNet · XGBoost · gain-scheduled PID · University of Bath, 2026

Problem

In Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF), a Metal Additive Manufacturing (MAM) process, melt pool depth is the primary determinant of defect formation. Existing in-situ monitoring captures only surface-level signatures; subsurface depth remains inaccessible in real time.

Approach

This project presents an ML depth estimator, trained on experimental data, as a real-time virtual sensor within a closed-loop system. Its output feeds a Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) controller that adjusts laser power to maintain a stable melt pool.

Results

The selected XGBoost model achieves strong predictive performance (R² = 0.9476 on the hold-out test set and mean CV R² = 0.8184).

Concrete compressive strength prediction

XGBoost · Random Forest · SVR · SHAP · University of Bath, 2025

Problem

Concrete compressive strength varies widely because of the heterogeneity in constituent proportions of its ingredients. There is a multivariate relationship between these mix parameters and compressive strength, making empirical calculation unfeasible. Existing destructive testing is high-cost and time-consuming. Can an ML model accurately and efficiently predict compressive strength?

Approach

Data input → data cleaning → univariate analysis → outlier detection → multivariate analysis → feature engineering → data splitting → train ML models → hyperparameter optimisation → test → model evaluation → Shapley Additive exPlanations reveal non-linear interdependencies.

Results

Bayesian optimisation was the strongest optimisation. XGBoost was the strongest model. SVR had the best generalisability.
